block_name: The Engineered Addictiveness of Social Media
short_summary: Platforms are built to maximize addictiveness
block_text:
Social media isn’t just a tool people happen to use. It’s a system built by teams of engineers and designers who understand human psychology—sometimes better than we understand ourselves. These platforms aren’t neutral. They’re carefully crafted to be as addictive as possible. The people behind them study how our brains work, especially how we respond to rewards, attention, and social approval. Their goal is simple: keep you coming back, again and again.

At the core of this design is dopamine. Every time you get a like, a comment, or a new follower, your brain gets a tiny hit of this chemical. Dopamine is the same neurotransmitter involved in gambling, eating sweets, or even using certain drugs. It’s what makes something feel rewarding. Social media platforms use this to their advantage. They create endless opportunities for you to chase that next little burst of pleasure. Notifications, red badges, and unpredictable rewards—all of it is meant to trigger your brain’s reward system.

But it goes deeper. The algorithms behind your feed are not just showing you what’s new. They’re constantly learning what grabs your attention, what makes you react, what keeps you scrolling. If you pause on a post, the system notices. If you react strongly—anger, excitement, envy—the algorithm learns. It starts to serve you more of what gets a response, even if it’s something that upsets you. The goal isn’t to make you happy. The goal is to keep you engaged, no matter what you feel.

This is why social media can feel so hard to put down. It’s not just about seeing what your friends are up to. It’s about being caught in a loop—one that’s been engineered to be as sticky as possible. The more you use it, the more the system adapts to you, making it even harder to step away. And for most people, this feels normal. It’s just how things are now. But there’s a reason some people choose to step outside this loop entirely—a reason that goes deeper than just wanting to be different.
